chapter: Follow-up questions, Bird and the Ellington sidemen
title: First piano teacher Miss Barrett, Wilson orchestra and giving up the bass
summary: Jones recalls Miss Barrett, the 50-75 piece Wilson Junior College orchestra, why he returned to piano from bass, and Marion Evans and Rudolph Schramm.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: Yeah. Have you happened to remember
the name of the lady who was your first piano teacher, since we were last taping?
I think her name was Miss Barrett, if I can remember, -- I have to remember her because she was tough.
(Laughter)
She was tough. She made me work at it. And I didn't know what she was doing at the time, but now I really appreciate it.
Was Miss Barrett in Chicago?
Yes.
Do you happen to remember her first name?
No, I can't remember her first name.
And you mentioned that Wilson Junior College had a symphony orchestra. How large was the orchestra?
Oh, we had -- there were about 50 to 75 pieces. And I was the bass player, one of the bass players. We had like four bass players, you know.
Uh-huh.
And we used to play operettas and things, you know. I thought I wanted to be a bass player, but in those times it cost too much money, so --
You mean to buy a bass?
Yeah. So the piano was still in the house, so I had to go back to piano, you know?
How do you feel now? Do you wish you had studied bass or kept with the bass or --
No, I like piano better.
You certainly seem to have a magnificent affinity for the piano.
Yeah, I like piano, because it's -- the knowledge you get from it. Bass, you only play one note at a time. And piano you play ten.
(Laughter)

Ten notes. You've got two hands there, you know. So consequently it's almost like orchestrating, you know. Of course in later years, since I've been writing, I don't write near the piano. I don't even touch the piano anymore because I had a couple of teachers in New York, very good teachers, that broke that habit that I had, you know, of orchestrating from the piano, because your mind is much better than your hands.
That was very interesting, when you mentioned that before. Did you -- I can't remember -- did you mention who the teachers were that weaned you from the piano?
Well, one was Marion Evans who was a great string writer and quite a friend.
I think you did mention him.
And then Rudolph Schramm at NYU. He was a Schillinger teacher, you know.
